notes.title: Infrastructure Architecture Overview
notes.content:
TechFlow AI — Infrastructure Architecture

Cloud Provider: AWS (us-west-2, Oregon)

Compute:
- Application: ECS Fargate (serverless containers)
  - Web service: 2 tasks (auto-scaling 2-6 based on CPU)
  - Worker service: 1 task (background jobs)
  - WebSocket service: 2 tasks (real-time collaboration)
- Container registry: ECR (private)
- Docker images: Node.js 20 Alpine base

Data Layer:
- Primary DB: RDS PostgreSQL 14 (db.r6g.xlarge)
  - Multi-AZ deployment
  - 2 read replicas (db.r6g.large)
  - Storage: 120GB gp3, auto-scaling to 500GB
  - PgBouncer for connection pooling
- Cache: ElastiCache Redis (cache.t4g.medium)
  - Used for: Session store, caching, Bull job queues
- Search: OpenSearch Service (2x t3.medium.search)
  - Tom's search feature (Elasticsearch-compatible)

Networking:
- VPC: 10.0.0.0/16
  - Public subnets: ALB, NAT Gateways
  - Private subnets: ECS tasks, RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch
- ALB: Application Load Balancer (HTTPS termination)
- CloudFront: CDN for static assets
- Route 53: DNS management

Security:
- WAF: Rate limiting, geo-blocking, SQL injection protection
- Security Groups: Strict inbound rules per service
- Secrets: AWS Secrets Manager (DB passwords, API keys)
- Encryption: At rest (AES-256) + in transit (TLS 1.3)
- IAM: Least privilege, role-based access

Monitoring:
- CloudWatch: Metrics, logs, alarms
- Datadog: APM, dashboards, alerting
- PagerDuty: On-call escalation (Priya primary, Alex secondary)

Cost: ~$8,500/month (trending from $6K in Nov — see cost optimization note)

notes.title: Kubernetes Migration Plan (Future)
notes.content:
Kubernetes Migration — Evaluation & Future Plan

Current State: ECS Fargate (serverless containers)
Proposed Future: EKS (Kubernetes) — NOT NOW, evaluation for future

Why Consider K8s:
- ECS is good for our current scale (3-6 containers)
- At 15+ services, ECS service mesh becomes complex
- K8s provides: Better service discovery, advanced scheduling, ecosystem tools
- Team hiring: More engineers know K8s than ECS

Why NOT Now:
- Current scale doesn't justify complexity
- Team is too small (I'm the only infra person)
- ECS Fargate is serving us well
- K8s overhead: etcd, control plane, node management
- Cost: EKS control plane ($72/month) + node overhead

Trigger Points for Migration:
- >10 services running
- >3 DevOps/SRE team members
- Need for advanced deployment patterns (canary, blue-green)
- Multi-region deployment requirements

Estimated Timeline: Q4 2026 or Q1 2027 (post-Series B, with larger team)

Prep Work (Can Do Now):
- Containerize everything cleanly (already done)
- Use Docker Compose for local dev (already done)
- Keep infrastructure as code (Terraform — already done)
- Standardize health checks and graceful shutdown (in progress)

Decision: Defer K8s migration. Revisit when we hit trigger points. ECS Fargate is the right choice for our current stage.

notes.title: CI/CD Pipeline Documentation
notes.content:
TechFlow — CI/CD Pipeline Documentation

Platform: GitHub Actions

Pipeline Stages:

1. PR Checks (runs on every PR):
- Lint (ESLint + Prettier): ~30s
- Type check (tsc --noEmit): ~45s
- Unit tests (Vitest): ~2 min
- Integration tests (database required): ~3 min
- Build check (next build): ~1 min
- Lighthouse CI (score check): ~2 min
- Security scan (Snyk): ~1 min
- Total PR pipeline: ~6 min

2. Merge to Main:
- All PR checks re-run
- E2E tests (Playwright): ~5 min
- Docker image build + push to ECR: ~3 min
- Deploy to staging: ~2 min
- Smoke tests against staging: ~1 min
- Total: ~12 min

3. Production Deploy (manual trigger by Alex or Mike):
- Pull latest staging image
- Run database migrations (if any)
- Blue-green deployment via ECS
- Health check: New tasks healthy before old tasks drain
- Smoke tests against production
- Notify #deployments Slack channel
- Total: ~5 min

Rollback:
- One-click rollback to previous task definition
- Database rollback: Manual (reversible migrations required)
- Time to rollback: <2 min

Secrets Management:
- GitHub Secrets: AWS credentials, Slack webhook
- Runtime secrets: AWS Secrets Manager (not baked into image)

Maintenance:
- GitHub Actions runners: GitHub-hosted (no self-hosted yet)
- Docker cache: Layer caching via GitHub Actions cache
- Dependency updates: Dependabot weekly PRs (auto-merge for patch)

Owner: Priya Sharma
Escalation: Alex Chen

notes.title: Auto-Scaling Configuration
notes.content:
TechFlow — Auto-Scaling Plan

Current Configuration:

ECS Web Service:
- Min tasks: 2
- Max tasks: 6
- Scale up: CPU > 70% for 3 min (add 1 task)
- Scale down: CPU < 30% for 10 min (remove 1 task)
- Cooldown: 5 min between scaling actions

ECS WebSocket Service:
- Min tasks: 2
- Max tasks: 4
- Scale up: Connection count > 500 per task
- Scale down: Connection count < 100 per task
- Note: WebSocket connections are sticky (can't drain mid-session)

ECS Worker Service:
- Min tasks: 1
- Max tasks: 3
- Scale up: Queue depth > 100 jobs pending
- Scale down: Queue depth = 0 for 15 min

RDS Read Replicas:
- Not auto-scaling (manual for now)
- Plan: Add 3rd replica if read traffic doubles

ElastiCache Redis:
- Not auto-scaling (single node sufficient)
- Monitor: Memory usage (currently 30% of 6.4GB)

Cost Impact of Scaling:
- Minimum (low traffic): 2 web + 2 ws + 1 worker = ~$350/month
- Maximum (peak): 6 web + 4 ws + 3 worker = ~$1,050/month
- Typical: 3 web + 2 ws + 1 worker = ~$500/month

Load Testing Results (k6, February 2026):
- 100 concurrent users: 3 web tasks sufficient
- 500 concurrent users: 5 web tasks needed
- 1000 concurrent users: 6 tasks (max) — borderline, need to increase max

Action Item: Increase max web tasks from 6 to 10 before any marketing push or Product Hunt launch.

notes.title: Secrets Management Policy
notes.content:
TechFlow — Secrets Management Policy

Principles:
1. Never store secrets in code or environment files committed to Git
2. Never log secrets (mask in logging library)
3. Rotate secrets quarterly (or immediately if compromised)
4. Least privilege: Each service gets only the secrets it needs

Storage:
- AWS Secrets Manager: Production secrets
  - Database credentials
  - API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, SendGrid, Stripe)
  - OAuth client secrets (NextAuth)
  - Elasticsearch credentials
- GitHub Secrets: CI/CD pipeline secrets
  - AWS access keys (deploy role)
  - Slack webhook URL
  - Snyk token

Access Control:
- Production secrets: Only the ECS task role can read them at runtime
- Developers: No direct access to production secrets
- Admin access: Priya + Alex only (for emergency rotation)
- Principle: Nobody should need to know the actual secret value

Rotation Schedule:
- Database passwords: Every 90 days (automated via Secrets Manager rotation)
- API keys: Every 90 days (manual — set calendar reminder)
- OAuth secrets: Annually (or on incident)
- TLS certificates: Auto-renewed via ACM (no manual rotation)

Incident Response:
- If a secret is suspected compromised:
  1. Rotate immediately (don't wait for confirmation)
  2. Deploy new secret to all services
  3. Audit access logs for unauthorized use
  4. Notify team in #security channel
  5. Post-incident: How was it exposed? Prevent recurrence.

Local Development:
- Use .env.local (gitignored)
- Developers use their own test API keys (not production)
- Database: Local Docker container (no connection to production)
- Template: .env.example with placeholder values

notes.title: Disaster Recovery Plan
notes.content:
TechFlow — Disaster Recovery Plan

RTO (Recovery Time Objective): 4 hours
RPO (Recovery Point Objective): 1 hour (max data loss)

Backup Strategy:
- RDS PostgreSQL:
  - Automated snapshots: Every 6 hours
  - Point-in-time recovery: Enabled (5-min granularity)
  - Cross-region backup: Daily snapshot copied to us-east-1
  - Retention: 30 days

- Redis (ElastiCache):
  - Daily snapshots (but Redis is ephemeral — can rebuild from DB)
  - Persistence: RDB snapshots every 15 min

- Elasticsearch (OpenSearch):
  - Automated snapshots: Daily at 2 AM UTC
  - Recovery: Restore from snapshot + reindex delta from DB
  - Full reindex time: ~10 min for current corpus

- Application Code:
  - Git (GitHub) is source of truth
  - Docker images stored in ECR (latest 10 versions retained)

Disaster Scenarios:

1. Single AZ failure:
- Impact: One ECS task, one DB replica may go offline
- Recovery: Automatic. Multi-AZ deployment handles failover.
- RTO: <5 min (automatic)

2. Full region failure (us-west-2 down):
- Impact: Everything offline
- Recovery: Deploy to us-east-1 from cross-region backup
- RTO: ~2-4 hours (manual process)
- Steps: Restore DB from cross-region snapshot, deploy ECS tasks, update DNS

3. Data corruption (bad migration, bug):
- Impact: Data loss or corruption in primary DB
- Recovery: Point-in-time recovery to before the corruption event
- RTO: ~30 min (restore to new instance, swap connection)
- RPO: Up to 5 min of data loss

4. Security breach:
- Impact: Unauthorized access to data
- Recovery: Isolate, rotate all credentials, assess damage
- Plan: Follow incident response playbook (see separate doc)

Testing:
- DR drill: Quarterly (last drill: January 15, 2026)
- Last drill result: Restored DB in 22 min, full service in 1 hour 45 min ✓

notes.title: Cost Optimization Analysis
notes.content:
AWS Cost Optimization — February 2026 Analysis

Current Monthly Cost: $8,500
Target: $7,000 (requested by Sarah/Carlos for board reporting)

Breakdown:
- ECS Fargate: $1,200 (compute for all services)
- RDS PostgreSQL: $2,800 (primary + 2 replicas)
- ElastiCache Redis: $350
- OpenSearch: $200 (Tom's search cluster)
- ALB + CloudFront: $400
- Data transfer: $350
- Secrets Manager + KMS: $50
- S3 (user uploads, backups): $300
- NAT Gateway: $250 (expensive for what it is)
- Miscellaneous (Route 53, CloudWatch, etc.): $200
- Datadog: $2,400 (APM for all services)

Optimization Opportunities:

1. Reserved Instances for RDS: -$600/month
   - Convert primary to 1-year reserved (37% discount)
   - Risk: Locked in for 1 year. Worth it — DB isn't changing.

2. Right-size read replicas: -$200/month
   - Currently db.r6g.large (overkill for read traffic)
   - Downgrade to db.r6g.medium (still plenty of capacity)

3. NAT Gateway consolidation: -$100/month
   - Currently 2 NAT Gateways (one per AZ)
   - Can use 1 for non-critical traffic, keep 2 for HA
   - Risk: Single point of failure for outbound traffic in one AZ

4. Datadog tier optimization: -$400/month
   - We're paying for Enterprise features we don't use
   - Downgrade 2 hosts from APM Pro to APM Standard
   - Keep APM Pro for production web service only

5. S3 lifecycle policies: -$50/month
   - Move old backups to Glacier after 30 days
   - Delete staging backups after 7 days

Total Potential Savings: $1,350/month
New Monthly Cost: ~$7,150 (close to target!)

Action Plan:
- March: Implement S3 lifecycle + Datadog downgrade (easy, low risk)
- April: Purchase RDS reserved instance (after confirming instance type is final)
- April: Right-size read replicas (after monitoring post-search-launch)
- Defer: NAT Gateway (risk vs. minimal savings)

Presenting to Sarah/Alex on March 8.

notes.title: Incident Postmortem — Feb 15 Participation
notes.content:
Incident Postmortem Participation — February 15, 2026

Role: Infrastructure monitoring (detected via alerting)

What Happened (from my perspective):
- 1:42 PM: Received PagerDuty alert — 'RDS connection pool utilization > 80%'
- 1:43 PM: Checked Datadog — confirmed connection exhaustion
- 1:44 PM: Notified Mike in Slack (he was already investigating from error rate spike)
- 1:48 PM: Mike identified the root cause (feature flag + aggressive auto-save)
- 1:52 PM: Mike disabled the feature flag
- 2:05 PM: Confirmed recovery from infrastructure side (connections draining normally)

My Action Items from This Incident:
1. Add alert at 80% connection pool utilization ✓ (DONE, same day)
   - Previously only had alert at 95% (too late)
   - New: Warning at 80%, Critical at 90%

2. Add connection pool dashboard to Datadog ✓ (DONE, Feb 16)
   - New panel: Active connections / Max connections (gauge)
   - Historical: Connection count over time

3. Review PgBouncer configuration
   - Max client connections: 500 (was sufficient before, but now tight)
   - Increased to 750 as buffer
   - Added monitoring for PgBouncer itself (wait time, active/idle clients)

Lessons for Me:
- The alert system worked. I got paged within 1 minute of the issue starting.
- But: I couldn't diagnose the application-level cause (that's Mike's domain).
- Need better runbook for 'connection exhaustion' scenario (what to check, in what order).
- Wrote runbook and added to our ops wiki.

notes.title: Vendor Evaluation — Datadog vs Grafana
notes.content:
Monitoring Vendor Evaluation — Datadog vs Grafana Cloud

Context: Current Datadog cost ($2,400/month) is our 3rd largest AWS-related expense. Evaluating alternatives.

Datadog (Current):
- Cost: $2,400/month (5 hosts APM, 15GB logs, custom metrics)
- Pros: All-in-one, excellent UI, great AWS integration, AI-assisted alerting
- Cons: Expensive, costs scale with infrastructure growth, vendor lock-in
- Estimate at 2x infra: $4,000+/month

Grafana Cloud:
- Cost: ~$800-1,200/month (estimated for our usage)
- Pros: Open source ecosystem, Prometheus/Loki/Tempo, lower cost at scale
- Cons: More setup work, less polished UI, need to integrate multiple tools
- Components: Grafana (dashboards), Prometheus (metrics), Loki (logs), Tempo (traces)

Self-Hosted Grafana Stack:
- Cost: ~$200/month (infrastructure only) + my time to maintain
- Pros: Cheapest, full control, no vendor lock-in
- Cons: Significant maintenance burden, I'm the only ops person
- NOT recommended at our stage

Recommendation: Stay with Datadog for now.

Reasoning:
- Switching cost is high (all dashboards, alerts, runbooks reference Datadog)
- I'm solo — can't afford time to migrate + maintain alternative
- Datadog's APM is genuinely better for debugging production issues
- Compromise: Optimize our Datadog plan (downgrade some hosts, reduce log retention)
- Revisit when we hire DevOps engineer and have bandwidth for migration

Cost optimization applied: $2,400 → $2,000/month (-$400, see cost optimization note)

notes.title: Interview Feedback — Previous DevOps Candidate
notes.content:
Interview Feedback — DevOps Engineer Candidate

Candidate: James Mitchell
Date: December 12, 2025
Role: DevOps Engineer (reporting to Priya)

Technical Screen (45 min):
- AWS knowledge: Good (EC2, RDS, ECS). Weak on serverless (Lambda, Fargate).

4. Culture fit: Seemed more interested in building complex infrastructure than solving business problems.

Positives:
- Good communicator, asked clarifying questions
- Docker knowledge was solid
- K8s knowledge specifically was deep (just not relevant to us)

Decision: No hire. Wait for a candidate who matches our actual stack (AWS + ECS + Terraform + GitHub Actions) and has a pragmatic 'right tool for the job' mindset.

notes.title: Deployment Runbook
notes.content:
TechFlow — Production Deployment Runbook
(Maintained by Priya Sharma)

Pre-Deployment Checklist:
☐ All CI checks passing on main
☐ E2E tests passing in staging
☐ No active incidents
☐ Not Friday afternoon (no Friday deploys unless emergency)
☐ At least 2 engineers available (deployer + someone to verify)
☐ Database migration reviewed (if any)

Deployment Steps:

1. Announce in #deployments: 'Starting production deploy of [commit SHA]'

2. If database migration:
   a. Run migration in production: `pnpm db:migrate:prod` (via ECS exec)
   b. Verify: Check migration status, no errors
   c. NOTE: Migrations must be backwards-compatible (old code must still work)

3. Trigger deployment:
   - GitHub Actions: Go to Actions > Deploy Production > Run workflow
   - Select: Branch = main, confirm

4. Monitor:
   - Watch ECS service events (new tasks launching)
   - Check: New tasks passing health checks
   - Check: Old tasks draining connections (2 min drain period)
   - Check: Datadog — no error rate spike
   - Check: Application logs — no new errors

5. Verify:
   - Hit production URL: https://app.techflow.ai
   - Test critical paths: Login, create document, search, save
   - Check: API health endpoint returns 200

6. Announce in #deployments: 'Deploy complete. All healthy. ✓'

Rollback Procedure:
1. If issues detected during deploy:
   - Go to ECS console > Service > Update
   - Set task definition to PREVIOUS revision
   - Click 'Force new deployment'
   - Time to rollback: <2 min
2. If database migration caused issues:
   - Run rollback migration: `pnpm db:rollback:prod`
   - Then rollback application (step 1)

Escalation:
- If deploy fails and you can't fix: Page Priya (PagerDuty)
- If Priya unavailable: Page Alex
- NEVER leave a broken deploy running. Always rollback first, investigate second.

Deploy Permissions:
- Can deploy: Alex Chen, Mike Torres, Priya Sharma
- Can approve (but not trigger): Lisa Nakamura, Tom Bradford

notes.title: Terraform Module Structure
notes.content:
TechFlow Infrastructure — Terraform Organization

Repo: github.com/techflow-ai/techflow-infra

Directory Structure:
```
terraform/
├── modules/
│   ├── networking/     # VPC, subnets, NAT, security groups
│   ├── database/       # RDS PostgreSQL, read replicas, PgBouncer
│   ├── cache/          # ElastiCache Redis
│   ├── compute/        # ECS cluster, services, task definitions
│   ├── search/         # OpenSearch domain
│   ├── cdn/            # CloudFront, S3 buckets
│   ├── monitoring/     # CloudWatch alarms, SNS topics
│   └── security/       # WAF, IAM roles, Secrets Manager
├── environments/
│   ├── staging/        # Staging configuration
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   ├── variables.tf
│   │   └── terraform.tfvars
│   ├── production/     # Production configuration
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   ├── variables.tf
│   │   └── terraform.tfvars
│   └── eu-west-1/      # Future: EU deployment
│       └── (planned)
└── global/             # Shared resources (Route53, ACM, ECR)
```

State Management:
- Backend: S3 + DynamoDB (state locking)
- State file per environment (no cross-env state)
- State bucket: techflow-terraform-state (versioned, encrypted)

Workflow:
1. Make changes in terraform/
2. Open PR with `terraform plan` output
3. Priya reviews plan
4. On merge: `terraform apply` (manual — not automated for safety)

Conventions:
- All resources tagged: Environment, Service, ManagedBy=terraform
- Naming: {service}-{environment}-{resource} (e.g., techflow-prod-rds)
- No inline resources — everything in modules
- Variables have descriptions and type constraints

Who Can Apply:
- Staging: Priya, Alex
- Production: Priya only (Alex can in emergency)
- Global: Priya only

notes.title: SSL/TLS Certificate Management
notes.content:
TechFlow — Certificate Management

Domains:
- techflow.ai (main)
- app.techflow.ai (application)
- api.techflow.ai (API)
- storybook.techflow.dev (component library)

Certificate Provider: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
- Auto-renewal: Yes (ACM handles this automatically for DNS-validated certs)
- Validation method: DNS (CNAME records in Route 53)
- Key algorithm: RSA 2048

Certificate Status (as of Feb 2026):
- *.techflow.ai: Valid until Nov 2026 (auto-renews)
- *.techflow.dev: Valid until Sep 2026 (auto-renews)

Where Certificates Are Used:
- ALB (HTTPS termination) — *.techflow.ai
- CloudFront distribution — *.techflow.ai (must be in us-east-1!)
- API Gateway (future) — api.techflow.ai

Monitoring:
- Alert: 30 days before expiry (P3 — shouldn't happen with auto-renewal)
- Alert: If renewal fails (P2 — check DNS validation records)

Notes:
- ACM certs are free (no cost)
- Cannot export ACM certs (they stay in AWS)
- If we need certs for non-AWS services: Use Let's Encrypt (certbot)
- CloudFront requires cert in us-east-1 region (even though we're in us-west-2)
